topics.title: Water resources of India: the big numbers

learn.hook: India has about one-sixth of the world's people but only about 4% of its water. Every drop matters!
points: Water is a cyclic, renewable resource, but its quantity is limited; demand is rising while quality is declining.

India accounts for about 2.45 per cent of the world's surface area and 4 per cent of its water resources, but about one-sixth of its population (16 per cent in NCERT's figure; 17.5 per cent in Census 2011).
Total water available from precipitation in a year is about 4,000 cubic km; availability from surface water and replenishable groundwater is 1,869 cubic km.
Only about 60 per cent of this can be put to beneficial use, so the total utilisable water resource is only 1,122 cubic km.

example.q: Show that about 60% of 1,869 cubic km gives the utilisable water figure.
steps: = 1,121.4 cubic km ≈ 1,122 cubic km.

learn.reallife: Chennai's 'Day Zero' scare in 2019, when reservoirs ran dry, showed how limited India's usable water really is.

learn.hook: The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak drain only about a third of India's area but carry about 60% of its surface water.
points: Surface water has four main sources: rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks.
India has about 10,360 rivers and tributaries longer than 1.6 km each; the mean annual flow in all river basins is estimated at 1,869 cubic km.
Due to topographical, hydrological and other constraints, only about 690 cubic km of surface water can be utilised.

Water flow in a river depends on the size of its catchment (river basin) and the rainfall within it. The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have extremely large catchments with high rainfall; though covering only about one-third of the country's area, they have about 60 per cent of its surface water resources.
Much of the annual flow of south Indian rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri has been harnessed, but this is yet to be done in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins.

example.q: Why do the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have so much more water than peninsular rivers?
steps: Flow depends on catchment size and rainfall in the catchment.
These rivers have huge catchments with high rainfall (and Himalayan snowmelt).
So they carry about 60% of India's surface water.

learn.reallife: Cauvery water-sharing disputes between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu arise because the river's flow is already heavily used.

learn.hook: In parts of Punjab, the water table has dropped so low that farmers must bore hundreds of feet. Groundwater is running out!
points: India's total replenishable groundwater resources are about 432 cubic km.
The Ganga and Brahmaputra basins have about 46 per cent of the total replenishable groundwater.
Groundwater utilisation is relatively high in river basins of the north-west and parts of south India — very high in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.
States like Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tripura and Maharashtra use groundwater at a moderate rate, while Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Kerala use only a small proportion of their potential.
If the present trend continues, demand will exceed supply; over-exploitation lowers the water table and can harm development and cause social disruption — so sustainable use is essential.

example.q: What share of the 432 cubic km of replenishable groundwater lies in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins (about 46%)? Work out the volume.

learn.reallife: The Atal Bhujal Yojana works with villages in water-stressed states like Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat to manage groundwater sustainably.

topics.title: Lagoons, backwaters and India's agrarian base

learn.hook: Kerala's backwaters, Odisha's Chilika and Bengal's coastal lakes hold huge amounts of water — but it is salty!
points: India has a vast and, in some states, highly indented coastline, which has led to the formation of many lagoons and lakes.
Kerala, Odisha and West Bengal have vast surface water resources in such lagoons and lakes.
The water in these water bodies is generally brackish, but it is used for fishing and for irrigating certain varieties of paddy crops and coconut.
India has traditionally been an agrarian economy; about two-thirds of its population has depended on agriculture, so water demand is dominated by farming.

example.q: Why can't lagoon water be used for drinking, though it is used for fishing and some paddy?
steps: Lagoon water is mixed with sea water — brackish.
Brackish water is unfit for drinking without treatment.
But some fish and salt-tolerant paddy and coconut can use it.
example.answer: It is brackish; only salt-tolerant uses are possible

learn.reallife: Chilika, Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, supports thousands of fishing families and migratory birds.

learn.hook: Out of every 100 litres of surface water India uses, about 89 go to farms. Industry gets just 2!
points: Agriculture accounts for most water use: 89 per cent of surface water and 92 per cent of groundwater utilisation.
Industry uses only 2 per cent of surface water and 5 per cent of groundwater.
The domestic sector uses 9 per cent of surface water — higher than its share of groundwater (3 per cent).
In future, demand from the industrial and domestic sectors is expected to increase with industrialisation and urbanisation.
A pie chart of sectoral use shows agriculture's huge slice in both surface and groundwater.

example.q: Using the sectoral shares, find the domestic share of groundwater use.
steps: Groundwater: agriculture 92% + industry 5% = 97%.
Domestic = 100 − 97 = 3%.

learn.reallife: Drip and sprinkler irrigation under 'Per Drop More Crop' (PMKSY) aim to cut agriculture's huge share of water use.

topics.title: Demand for irrigation and its problems

learn.hook: Punjab irrigates over 85% of its net sown area — and now worries about arsenic, fluoride and a vanishing water table.
points: Irrigation is needed because rainfall is unevenly distributed in space and time: large tracts (north-western India, Deccan plateau) are rainfall-deficient and drought-prone; winter and summer are dry in most parts; even in high-rainfall states like West Bengal and Bihar, breaks or failure of monsoon cause dry spells.
Some crops like rice, sugarcane and jute need a lot of water; multiple cropping is possible only with irrigation; HYV crops need regulated moisture.

Irrigation raises productivity: in Punjab, Haryana and western UP, more than 85 per cent of net sown area is irrigated, and wheat and rice there are grown mainly with irrigation, largely from wells and tube wells.

Problems of excessive irrigation: over-drawing of groundwater lowers the water table; fluoride concentration has increased in Rajasthan and Maharashtra and arsenic in West Bengal and Bihar; intensive irrigation also raises soil salinity.

example.q: Give three reasons why a farmer in Haryana relies on tube wells.
steps: Haryana gets limited rainfall concentrated in a few months.
Wheat (rabi) is grown in the dry winter.
HYV crops and multiple cropping need assured, regulated water.
example.answer: Scanty seasonal rain, dry-season crops and HYV/multiple cropping needs

topics.title: Emerging water problems: availability and pollution

learn.hook: The same Yamuna that is clear near its source becomes one of India's most polluted rivers after Delhi. What goes wrong?
points: Per capita availability of water is declining due to the increase in population.
Available water resources are also getting polluted by industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents, which limits usable water further.
Water quality refers to the purity of water, i.e. water without unwanted foreign substances; pollution happens when toxic substances enter lakes, streams, rivers, oceans and other water bodies.

Polluted water harms aquatic life and human health. CPCB data show organic and bacterial contamination as the main pollution source in rivers; the Yamuna is most polluted between Delhi and Etawah, and the Ganga is highly polluted at Kanpur and Varanasi; other polluted rivers include the Sabarmati at Ahmedabad, Gomti at Lucknow and Musi at Hyderabad.

example.q: If a city's water supply stays at 300 crore litres a day while its population rises from 1.5 crore to 2 crore, what happens to per capita supply?
steps: Before: 300 ÷ 1.5 = 200 litres per person per day.
After: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 litres per person per day.
Per capita availability falls by 50 litres.
example.answer: Falls from 200 to 150 litres per person per day

learn.reallife: The Namami Gange programme sets up sewage treatment plants in Kanpur, Varanasi and other cities to clean the Ganga.

topics.title: Water conservation: pollution control and recycling

learn.hook: A Bengaluru apartment treats its own sewage and uses it to flush toilets and water gardens — saving lakhs of litres of fresh water.
points: Declining availability and rising demand make conservation and effective management of water essential.

Strategies: water-saving technologies and methods, prevention of pollution, watershed development, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and reuse, conjunctive use of surface and groundwater, and long-term planning.

Prevention of pollution: the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), with State Pollution Control Boards, monitors water quality. Laws like the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 have not been implemented effectively; public awareness is needed.

Recycle and reuse: lower-quality reclaimed waste water can be used by industries for cooling and fire-fighting; in cities, water from bathing and washing utensils (and vehicle washing) can be used for gardening — reducing demand for fresh water.

example.q: Suggest two ways a factory and two ways a household can recycle water.
steps: Factory: use treated waste water for cooling; use it for fire-fighting.
Household: use bathing/utensil water for gardening; reuse vehicle-washing water for plants.
example.answer: Factory — cooling, fire-fighting; household — gardening with used water

learn.reallife: Many Indian cities now mandate sewage treatment plants in large housing societies and reuse treated water for non-drinking purposes.

learn.hook: Ralegan Siddhi, a drought-hit village in Maharashtra, turned green by building check dams and planting trees — through people's own efforts.
points: Watershed management means efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater resources: preventing runoff, and storing and recharging groundwater through percolation tanks, recharge wells etc.
In a broad sense it includes conservation, regeneration and judicious use of all natural (land, water, plants, animals) and human resources within a watershed; community participation is essential.

Haryali: a Central Government–sponsored watershed project enabling rural people to conserve water for drinking, irrigation, fisheries and afforestation; executed by Gram Panchayats with people's participation.

Neeru-Meeru ('Water and You') in Andhra Pradesh and Arvary Pani Sansad in Alwar (Rajasthan) built water-harvesting structures like percolation tanks, dug-out ponds (johads) and check dams through people's participation.
Ralegan Siddhi (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra) is a celebrated example of village-led watershed development that ended water scarcity.

learn.hook: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings — and Chennai's groundwater levels improved in response!
points: Rainwater harvesting is a method of capturing and storing rainwater for various uses; it is also used to recharge groundwater aquifers.
It is a low-cost and eco-friendly technique for preserving every drop of water by guiding rainwater to bore wells, pits and wells.
Traditional methods: lakes, ponds and irrigation tanks in rural areas; in Rajasthan, rainwater is stored in kunds or tankas (covered underground tanks) near houses or villages.

Benefits: increases water availability, checks the declining groundwater table, improves groundwater quality by diluting contaminants like fluoride and nitrates, prevents soil erosion and flooding, and arrests salt-water intrusion in coastal areas if used to recharge aquifers.
Tamil Nadu has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory in all houses — no building can be constructed without them.

example.q: A rooftop of 100 sq m receives 800 mm (0.8 m) of rain a year. Ideally, how many litres can be harvested? (1 cubic m = 1,000 litres)
steps: Volume = area × rainfall = 100 × 0.8 = 80 cubic m.

topics.title: National Water Policy and Jal Kranti Abhiyan

learn.hook: When water is scarce, who gets it first — farms, factories or families? India's National Water Policy answers: drinking water comes first.
points: The National Water Policy (2002) stipulates water allocation priorities: drinking water gets the top priority, followed by irrigation, hydropower and other uses such as industry and navigation.

Other NWP features: irrigation and multipurpose projects should include a drinking-water component; groundwater exploitation should be regulated; water quality should be improved; water should be conserved by efficient use; farmers and stakeholders should participate in management.

Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015–16): aims to ensure water security through per capita availability of water; water-scarce villages in each district are selected as 'Jal Grams' for integrated water security plans; model command areas are developed; it promotes traditional and modern conservation with people's participation.
Exam focus: water figures (4,000; 1,869; 1,122; 432 cubic km), sectoral use, causes of declining water resources, emerging problems, watershed management and rainwater harvesting.
